topic.title: Psychology: The Jaipur Memory Project: retraining people to forget safely
topic.focus: The Jaipur Memory Project: retraining people to forget safely

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-8. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: A clinic in India tackles trauma
sections.text: In 2014, Dr. Rajesh Patel established a clinic in Jaipur, India, specialising in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) among refugees and accident survivors. His team found that 73% of patients experienced debilitating flashbacks that prevented them from working or sleeping. Unlike most trauma clinics, Patel's approach was based not on reinforcing memories but on weakening them — a controversial technique called reconsolidation therapy. After each patient recalled a traumatic event in a safe setting, they took a beta-blocker to suppress the emotional response while sleeping. Over twelve weeks, most patients reported a 60% reduction in flashback intensity.

sections.heading: How the memory weakens
sections.text: Neuroscientists had understood since 2000 that memories become unstable when recalled. A team at McGill University in Montreal discovered that during this window of instability, the brain's emotional tag can be rewritten. When Dr. Patel's patients took propranolol, a beta-blocker commonly used for high blood pressure, it blocked the hormone adrenaline — the chemical that cements fear into memory during sleep. By interrupting this process just once per week for twelve weeks, the clinic achieved results comparable to years of traditional talk therapy. The key was timing: the drug had to be taken within six hours of recalling the trauma, and patients had to sleep within four hours of taking it.

sections.heading: Challenges and ethics
sections.text: The clinic treated 340 patients between 2014 and 2019. Of these, 76% showed significant improvement, while 14% experienced no change, and 10% reported adverse effects including numbness or emotional detachment. International review boards questioned whether it was ethical to alter memories without the person's full understanding of what they would lose. In 2018, the Indian Medical Council temporarily suspended the treatment pending further review. Patient testimonies were mixed: some described liberation from intrusive thoughts, while others felt they had lost an important part of their identity.

sections.heading: Expansion to other countries
sections.text: By 2021, similar programs had started in Bangkok, Buenos Aires, and Johannesburg. The International Society of Trauma Psychology endorsed reconsolidation therapy for PTSD in 2022, but only under strict protocols. Treatment costs ranged from $2,000 in India to $8,000 in North America, making access highly unequal. Insurance companies in the United States began covering the treatment in 2023, but only after proving symptom relief lasted at least two years.

sections.heading: The larger question
sections.text: Dr. Patel published his final cohort analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry in 2024, concluding that selective memory weakening represented neither a cure nor a complete erasure, but rather a recalibration of emotional intensity. He warned against overusing the technique on minor traumas or on patients who had not consented fully. As artificial intelligence systems began to replicate this model in 2023, ethicists raised concerns about whether machines could ever make the subtle judgments about which memories were safe to weaken.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — A clinic in India tackles trauma
In 2014, Dr. Rajesh Patel established a clinic in Jaipur, India, specialising in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) among refugees and accident survivors. His team found that 73% of patients experienced debilitating flashbacks that prevented them from working or sleeping. Unlike most trauma clinics, Patel's approach was based not on reinforcing memories but on weakening them — a controversial technique called reconsolidation therapy. After each patient recalled a traumatic event in a safe setting, they took a beta-blocker to suppress the emotional response while sleeping. Over twelve weeks, most patients reported a 60% reduction in flashback intensity.

Paragraph 2 — How the memory weakens
Neuroscientists had understood since 2000 that memories become unstable when recalled. A team at McGill University in Montreal discovered that during this window of instability, the brain's emotional tag can be rewritten. When Dr. Patel's patients took propranolol, a beta-blocker commonly used for high blood pressure, it blocked the hormone adrenaline — the chemical that cements fear into memory during sleep. By interrupting this process just once per week for twelve weeks, the clinic achieved results comparable to years of traditional talk therapy. The key was timing: the drug had to be taken within six hours of recalling the trauma, and patients had to sleep within four hours of taking it.

Paragraph 3 — Challenges and ethics
The clinic treated 340 patients between 2014 and 2019. Of these, 76% showed significant improvement, while 14% experienced no change, and 10% reported adverse effects including numbness or emotional detachment. International review boards questioned whether it was ethical to alter memories without the person's full understanding of what they would lose. In 2018, the Indian Medical Council temporarily suspended the treatment pending further review. Patient testimonies were mixed: some described liberation from intrusive thoughts, while others felt they had lost an important part of their identity.

Paragraph 4 — Expansion to other countries
By 2021, similar programs had started in Bangkok, Buenos Aires, and Johannesburg. The International Society of Trauma Psychology endorsed reconsolidation therapy for PTSD in 2022, but only under strict protocols. Treatment costs ranged from $2,000 in India to $8,000 in North America, making access highly unequal. Insurance companies in the United States began covering the treatment in 2023, but only after proving symptom relief lasted at least two years.

Paragraph 5 — The larger question
Dr. Patel published his final cohort analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry in 2024, concluding that selective memory weakening represented neither a cure nor a complete erasure, but rather a recalibration of emotional intensity. He warned against overusing the technique on minor traumas or on patients who had not consented fully. As artificial intelligence systems began to replicate this model in 2023, ethicists raised concerns about whether machines could ever make the subtle judgments about which memories were safe to weaken.
